div.head: Chapter 1
div.p: These doubts contain within themselves all the difficulty of the matter treated concerning the Indies, and through their truthful resolution, if God should see fit to grant light and favor to answer them in accordance with his law and commandment, there will without doubt be uncovered and made known an abyss of most pernicious errors that have persisted in Spain until this day since that new Indian world was discovered, to the detriment of the greater part of humankind that we found living within it. And consequently, the certainty of the danger will become apparent that many of us have incurred: some through crass or willful ignorance, others through affected ignorance (which is the refusal to be taught or to receive instruction in what they did not know); and yet others, the majority, through pure and consummate malice. All these failings had their origin either in ignoring, or in caring little about, the following principles — if indeed they were not ignored altogether.

In order to respond, then, to the said doubts, invoking divine grace and trusting solely in that supreme aid, I will say two things as briefly as I am able, though the matter is most weighty and would require far more time and even greater capacity of mind, referring the reader to my many treatises, in which, as many learned men, lawyers, theologians, and jurists who affirm it attest, I have made evident what I will say here. The first, then, will be to set forth certain principles most true and most firm, which must of necessity be presupposed in this dispute, and whoever should deny any of them may rightly be excluded from it.

The second will be to draw certain responsive conclusions toward the resolution of each doubt, submitting in this way all that I may say and write to the final determination of the Holy Church, or to its head, who is the Roman Pontiff.

First Principle. All unbelievers, of whatever sect or religion they may be, or on account of whatever sins they may have, with respect to natural and divine law and to what is called the law of nations, justly hold and possess lordship over those things which they have acquired without harm to others; and likewise with the same justice they possess their principalities, kingdoms, states, dignities, jurisdictions, and dominions.

This principle is proved with respect to lordship over things by that passage of Genesis 1: "let us make" etc., and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and the beasts of the whole earth, and further: fill the earth and subdue it and have dominion over the fish, etc. And Psalm 8, speaking of man, "you have subjected all things," it says, "under his feet," etc. And Psalm 113: "the heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but the earth he has given to the children of men." And the Philosopher, in book 9 of the Ethics: we are in some manner the end of all things, and we make use of all that exists as though for our own sake. And in book 1 of the Politics, he says that the possession of external things is for man just and natural, and gives the example of the hunting of animals, etc.

As for jurisdictional dominion, principalities, kingdoms, states, and the governance of men over other men, it is likewise proved to be of natural law in the following way. When something is natural to another thing, everything is also natural to it by necessity without which that thing cannot be had or attained, because nature will not be lacking in necessary things, as the Philosopher teaches in book 3 of De anima. Now it is the case that for men to live together with others, a political and social life, as in towns and cities, is natural to men, according to the same Philosopher in book 1 of the Politics, and reason confirms this, namely: because for a man to live alone, or a household of husband and wife and children alone, could not sustain itself nor survive for long on account of the many needs that arise, which one person or a few cannot remedy and supply. Therefore everything that is necessary for the sustenance of that company or society will be natural to it and owed to it by natural law. And this is, and is chief among other things, to have someone who rules and governs that company and community and bears responsibility for the common good: for when many are gathered together without anyone to rule and govern them, confusion would arise, as is plain; and consequently the community would dissolve and could not be preserved, contrary to what nature intends by giving men a natural inclination to live together. And this Solomon shows in Proverbs 11: "where there is no governor, the people will fall." This ruler or governor can be none other than the one whom the whole company or community chose at the outset, or, where none has been chosen, the one they will choose, ut ff. de origi. juris. l. de inde cum essent, et § novissime, et 93. dist. c. legimus. Et quod nota in l. ex hoc iure ff. de Iusti. et iur.

And the one so chosen holds full jurisdiction, pure and mixed authority, when he recognizes no other as his superior, as all free kings do, as the jurists treat at length in the said l. ex hoc iure and in the chapter que in ecclesia 4, de consti., and in other places. Therefore to have a king, or rector, or whatever he may be called, in each kingdom, or city, or community assembled to live in a political manner, is for men absolutely and universally, believers or unbelievers alike, natural and of natural law, just as what is natural to each species of things is natural to all of them in common and to each one in particular: natural to men in general, and natural alike to unbelievers as to believers, since all are of one species and nature, the faithful being no more human as regards nature than the unfaithful, as appears from 1. dist. t. Jus naturale. It is likewise proved by the law of nations, which is common to all peoples, faithful or unfaithful, that iure omnes fere omnes gentes utuntur, capit. jus gentium, 1a. dist., l. ex hoc iure, already cited: ibi dispersae sunt gentes et facta sunt regna, etc., scilicet per populi electionem.

It appears also because Sacred Scripture, which speaks neither idly nor superfluously, names as kings in countless places in the Old and New Testaments those unbelievers who govern and governed the kingdoms of the unbelievers. And setting aside all other instances, consider what is read in Daniel 2, where Daniel, acknowledging Nebuchadnezzar, the most wicked idolater, as a king established by God: "You are a king of kings: and the God of heaven has given to you the kingdom, and strength, and power, and glory," etc.

From this comes what Saint Augustine, in the Questions on the Old and New Testament, question 35, says: By what reason does David call Saul, after God had withdrawn from him, the anointed of the Lord, and pay him honor? David was not unaware that the divine tradition lay in the office of the royal order; therefore he honors Saul, who was placed in that same tradition, lest he appear to do injury to one who decreed honor to those in such orders. For he bears the image of God, as a bishop bears that of Christ. Therefore, for as long as he remains within that tradition, he is to be honored, whether or not on his own account, at least for the sake of the order. Hence the Apostle, Romans 13: "be subject to higher powers: for there is no power but from God; and those that are, are ordained by God." Hence it is that we honor even a pagan who nonetheless holds power, though he himself may be unworthy, holding God's order while giving thanks to the devil: for power demands it, because it is deserving of honor. For it was for this reason that the dream of the famine was revealed to Pharaoh, and that Nebuchadnezzar, while others stood with him, alone saw the Son of God in the furnace of fire, not on account of his own merit, who wished to be worshipped in an idol, but on account of the merit of the royal order. Thus Augustine formally.

And so it appears that the kings of the unbelievers, however much they may be idolaters and most wicked, are by natural and divine law and by the law of nations true kings, and are owed the kingdom and the empire and the strength and the glory, that is to say: the excellence, honor and reverence, and the royal order; because for as long as they remain in that supreme state and dignity, they represent the image of God who instituted such a state, and thus it belongs to them with that authority to be kings. Therefore, whatever unbelievers, of whatever sect or religion they may be, justly hold and possess lordship over their things and over their states and dignities and kingdoms, and are kings by natural and divine law and by the law of nations. And on this Saint Thomas, 2a 2ae, q. 10, a. 10, and on the epistle 1 Corinthians, c. 6, says that it would be against divine law to prevent subjects, even Christian ones, from appearing as often as they are summoned before infidel princes or judges. Thus far he.
We call that person a king to whom the supreme power and jurisdiction of governance is entrusted by the people, community, or kingdom.

Corollary. From this it follows plainly that whoever steals or robs the things of unbelievers, and far more so whoever usurps their states, dignities, jurisdictions, and dominions without just cause, commits theft and rapine. Of this truth, no one who is not foolish and without free judgment will doubt in any way.
